question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: Ensemble suggests a 67% chance the UK will raise the qualifying period to 10 years, but objections reveal legislative, transitional, and rollout risks that could delay or limit universality by May 2026.
Phased rollout and exemptions mean many routes wouldn't reach a full 10-year baseline by May 2026, reducing the likelihood of universal application by that date.
Policy momentum is toward a 10-year baseline with a spring 2026 rollout signal, but as of March 1, 2026 the change is not law and retroactivity remains unsettled.
The final probability is adjusted downward from the ensemble to reflect these downside risks while preserving the overall directional trend.

justification.critique_assessment: The objections are valid and highlight genuine risk factors (legislation timing, transitional protections, phased rollout) that justify a downward adjustment from the ensemble; none imply impossibility.
justification.adjustment: Reduced from 0.67 to 0.60 to reflect downside risks from legislative delay, transitional uncertainties, and non-universal rollout, while maintaining the overall trend toward a 10-year baseline.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy reform proposals to set a baseline 10-year qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR) / settlement, with an 'earned settlement' concept; announced November 2025 and undergoing consultation during early 2026.

sources.claim: The government announced more details of a proposal on 20 November 2025 to set a baseline 10-year qualifying period for settlement, with a 12-week consultation through February 2026 and potential implementation from April 2026 if adopted.
Migration Observatory analysis suggests the reforms would establish a 10-year baseline route to settlement, with variations by category.
GOV.UK explains the Long Residence route requiring 10 years of continuous lawful residence, illustrating the relevance of a 10-year threshold in settlement policy.
The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from the current 5 years to 10 years, with exceptions for certain groups.

Migration Observatory explains the proposed 10-year baseline for settlement as part of the earned settlement reform and notes the public consultation running through February 2026, with many measures designed to lengthen waiting periods.

The House of Commons Library notes the earned settlement consultation is seeking views on whether the increase will apply to people already in the UK, and that no decision has been taken on that point.

Littler reports the November 2025 open consultation on earned settlement, proposing a 10-year standard qualifying period with a phased rollout anticipated from April 2026, ending consultation in February 2026.
Taylor Wessing summarizes the Home Office’s announcement of a major consultation on increasing the settlement qualifying period.
The GOV.UK consultation states the standard qualifying period for settlement will rise to 10 years as the baseline, with potential reductions based on integration, contribution, and residence.

House of Commons Library notes that the May 2025 immigration white paper proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for permanent residence from five to ten years, with final decisions after consultation.

Electronic Immigration Network reports the Home Office opened a public consultation in November 2025 on an earned settlement model; the standard ILR qualifying period would increase to 10 years, with changes expected to begin implementing in April 2026.
Guardian coverage notes the government's proposal to extend the settlement waiting period from five to ten years as part of the immigration white paper.
